Theme

School & learning

literature noun

written works, especially as an art

also letters, Latin literature, Greek literature, literary, writings

classical

Cic. Tusc. 1.3: omnī litterārum genere
Cic. Leg. 1.5: abest historia litterīs nostrīs (Lewis & Short)

litterae, litterārum f. pl.

noun, first declension, plural

literature, letters

The plural of littera, a letter of the alphabet, and so also a letter (epistle), a document, an account book, and learning (litterīs studēre). An adjective or the context makes it literature: Graecae, Latīnae litterae; Graecae dē philosophiā litterae, Greek philosophical literature (Cic. Div. 2.5).

Other words

  • scrīpta, scrīptōrum n. pl. — writings, works

    noun, second declension, plural · also used · classical · Cic. de Orat. 2.194: in scrīptīs relictum (Lewis & Short); Traupman 32, 409

    What someone has written: a writer’s works rather than literature at large.

  • litterātūra, litterātūrae f. — literature (modern use)

    noun, first declension · avoid · modern · Quint. 2.1.4: grammaticē, quam in Latīnum trānsferentēs litterātūram vocāvērunt

    Common in modern Latin for literature, but classically it is writing in letters (Cic. Part. 26), the alphabet (Tac. A. 11.13), grammar and philology (Quint. 2.1.4) and, late, learning (Tert.): Lewis & Short.

Examples

  • Doctrīnā Graecia nōs et omnī litterārum genere superābat

    In learning and in every kind of literature Greece surpassed usCic. Tusc. 1.3

  • abest historia litterīs nostrīs

    history is missing from our literatureCic. Leg. 1.5 (Lewis & Short)

See also book, author, history.
